title: Duck Confit
subtitle: Duck legs cured in salt then slow-cooked in fat until silky
excerpt: The ancient French preservation technique that produces the most tender, richly flavoured duck you will ever eat. Patience and low heat are the only tools you need.
sourceNotes: Traditional French preservation technique from Gascony, southwest France.

recipe.freezeNotes: Store cooked legs submerged in fat in the fridge for up to 4 weeks, or freeze for 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and keep in the fat for weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be started at least 12 hours ahead for the salt cure. Better with 24 hours.

content.text: This serves 4 and takes about 12 hours curing plus 2 hours 30 minutes cooking time. The thing to watch during cooking is the fat temperature: it should barely shimmer, never bubble. A proper confit is poached in fat, not fried in it.
Do not skip the salt cure. It draws out excess moisture, seasons the meat all the way through, and gives the finished confit its characteristic firm texture that stays moist under the skin.
Rub the duck legs all over with salt, garlic, pepper, thyme, and crushed bay leaves. Cover and refrigerate for at least 12 hours, or up to 24 hours.
Heat the oven to 140C. Rinse the duck legs under cold water to remove the cure. Pat very dry with kitchen paper.
Place the duck legs in the dutch oven and pour over the oil. The legs should be nearly submerged.
Heat on the hob over low heat until you see the first tiny bubbles rising. Transfer to the oven.
Cook for 2 hours 15 minutes. The fat should barely shimmer throughout. Check every 30 minutes.
The duck is ready when the meat pulls away from the bone easily. Remove from the fat.
To serve crispy, place skin-side down in a hot dry frying pan over high heat for 5-6 minutes until the skin crisps and browns. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Duck meat is dry and tough despite long cooking
items.cause: Fat was too hot and the duck fried rather than confited
items.fix: Temperature must stay at 140C or below - use a thermometer in the fat if possible

items.symptom: Skin will not crisp when finishing in the pan
items.cause: Too much moisture on the skin or pan not hot enough
items.fix: Pat the skin completely dry before putting in a very hot dry pan with no added fat

items.symptom: Meat is still pink near the bone after 2 hours
items.cause: Oven temperature too low or legs very large
items.fix: Return to the oven for another 30 minutes and check again

content.text: Duck confit comes from Gascony in southwest France, a region known for its duck and goose farming. The technique was originally about preservation: before refrigeration, meats cured in salt and stored under fat could last months. Today it is made purely for the unmatched texture and flavour it produces. Duck confit is a cornerstone ingredient in cassoulet and is served across the bistros of southwest France.
